reviews.text: Equally important is that the film avoids oversimplistic condemnations of the Iranian regime, showing that oppression can be propagated unconsciously, even by those who are at the bottom of society.
reviews.author: Angelos Koutsourakis

reviews.text: It touches on a reality of life that transcends any political or cultural barrier while also offering some thought-provoking insight into the religious laws and social structure of that part of the world.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: A Separation stimulates discussion about how the characters behave and how we feel about their choices.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: A Separation is an educational and sympathetic inside look at the way things work in Iran...
reviews.author: David Bax

reviews.text: A Separation provides one of the few glimpses that Americans and others in the West will have into the reality of Iranian life.
reviews.author: David Walsh

reviews.text: Rarely are family dramas as thematically or structurally complex as A Separation. Pair that with the fact that it is very well acted and intelligently photographed, and you have an extraordinary film.
reviews.author: Jordan M. Smith

reviews.text: The beauty of A Separation, and what one can only hope will help sell it to American audiences, is the universality of its themes, messages and conflicts.
reviews.author: Richard Propes

reviews.text: A stressful watch but worthwhile look at 2 marriages in Iran
reviews.author: Rachel Wagner

reviews.text: For fans of the sort of world cinema that plunges you into the essence of life in another reality, A Separation is an intense, immersive dip into contemporary Iranian life.
reviews.author: Felicia Feaster

reviews.text: [T]he X Factor in A Separation lies with its cast, bringing the extraordinary out of the seemingly ordinary.
reviews.author: Katie Smith-Wong

reviews.text: Farhadi discovers simple yet deeply human truths - that the divides that so often separate us can seem so impossibly wide are never quite as far as we imagine.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: Cleverly, A Separation doesn't conspicuously proselytise about its socio-political import; it is largely concerned with matters of the family that to some degree are universal
reviews.author: PJ Nabarro

reviews.text: The quiet, staggering power of "A Separation" is in the realization that navigating the politics of government or of family are tasks of equal scale and equally treacherous.
reviews.author: Stephen Saito

reviews.text: Just as nuanced, but with a bigger emotional punch, is the rest of this Rashomon-like tale of right and wrong, life and death, actions and consequences, all of which reveal various particulars of life in Tehran.
reviews.author: Kelly Jane Torrance

reviews.text: Writer/director Asghar Farhadi delivers a complex and honest portrayal of two families in modern-day Tehran. It is a challenging and heartbreaking film that deserves an audience.
reviews.author: Kiko Martinez

reviews.text: The complexity of the characters is wonderful; as a viewer you in one scene enraged at their actions then following a plot twist in the next scene you are wholeheartedly sympathizing with them.
reviews.author: Joseph Walsh

reviews.text: A Separation is a deeply empathetic movie. It feels for all of its characters even as they act in self-serving or self-deceiving ways.
reviews.author: Eve Tushnet

reviews.text: A Separation is a movie that keeps expanding, like one of those paper pellets that, when you drop it in water, blossoms into a flower.
reviews.author: John Powers

reviews.text: Simply exceptional. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Laura Hiros

reviews.text: With "A Separation," Iranian director Asghar Farhadi has managed something increasingly difficult and unusual - pleasing audiences both at home and in the West.
reviews.author: Steve Erickson

reviews.text: A Separation is one of the year's most accomplished films, and like so many films we might characterize as "accomplished," it hasn't garnered actual detractors. It merely fosters a coterie of skeptics.
reviews.author: Michael Sicinski

reviews.text: A Separation ends on the perfect note, a nearly impossible decision whose weight is left on our shoulders while the credits roll.
reviews.author: Derek Smith

reviews.text: Brilliantly [Asghar Farhadi] has posited his questions and dilemmas so that they are open-ended, depending entirely upon what the viewer brings to the table in terms of past experience and personal emotional involvement.
reviews.author: Neely Swanson

reviews.text: Its familiar and informal tone has accomplished what few films do: to be a hit among critics and less demanding moviegoers. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Fernanda Solórzano

reviews.text: A Separation achieves a delicate balance between the foreign and the familiar.
reviews.author: Eleanor Ringel Cater

reviews.text: Although its surface impartiality helped the film get past officious censors, underneath is a more complex picture.
reviews.author: Francesca Steele

reviews.text: It's ferociously wise, gripping, unsettling and acted with unerring conviction.
reviews.author: Michael Atkinson

reviews.text: As pure entertainment, "A Separation" is flawless. But as social commentary, one could infer a conservative agenda.
reviews.author: Martin Tsai

reviews.text: You cannot watch the film without feeling kinship with the characters and admitting their decency as well as their mistakes.
reviews.author: David Thomson

reviews.text: Ambiguous endings can work for some films, but it doesn't here. Still, the powerful performances and near seamless screenplay leave little else to be desired. A Separation deserves its Oscar.
reviews.author: Matt Kelemen

reviews.text: A case study in how simplicity can produce spectacular results that extend far beyond a film's budget.
reviews.author: Erick Weber

reviews.text: [A] flawless domestic portrait.
reviews.author: Alice Tynan

reviews.text: ... a complex and nuanced movie about the ... the collapse of a relationship between intelligent people of good will. It is heartbreaking and subtle, the sort of film that some folks say isn't made often or well enough by the usual Hollywood suspects.
reviews.author: Philip Martin

reviews.text: A Separation infuses a great insight into modern Iran with a powerful insight into the human condition - this demonstrates the power and poetic potential of cinematic drama. It's a MUST see.
reviews.author: Blake Howard

reviews.text: Writer-director Asghar Farhadi performs some kind of miracle with the tension and complexity he produces from such a simple set-up.
reviews.author: Mark Pfeiffer

reviews.text: ...riveting, enormously resonant and impressively acted...
reviews.author: Aaron Yap

reviews.text: Fahardi's accomplishment is to have brought to the screen a group of equally complex, equally flawed, and equally human characters whose only real problem is that they must live life with each other.
reviews.author: Simon Weaving

reviews.text: Offers an unwritten ending that must be decided by each viewer.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: ... subtlety and a sense of profound decency ...
reviews.author: Jim Lane

reviews.text: A clever, insightful and heartfelt examination of human frailty that makes watching subtitles seem like a breeze.
reviews.author: Dan Lybarger

reviews.text: It's fast paced, exciting, thrilling, edgy, moving, engaging, and - in its portrait of a justice system almost radically alien to the one I live under - absolutely fascinating.
reviews.author: CJ Johnson

reviews.text: Although the film might serve as a portrait of Iran's two conflicting social groups as reflected in the Green movement/Ahmadinejad clashes, it is much more about moral contradictions that any society has to face. A masterpiece.
reviews.author: Louis Proyect

reviews.text: It's the little moments in Farhadi's film that are its most important, speaking every bit as loudly as its big, narrative-driving moments.
reviews.author: Mike Scott

reviews.text: Dynamically shot and paced like a thriller, the film has the density and moral prickliness of a good novel.
reviews.author: Jon Frosch

reviews.text: If any one film can re-inject life into an entire national cinema, it's A Separation.
reviews.author: John Thomason

reviews.text: You may also find that some aspects of this very foreign story seem disturbingly not all that foreign.
reviews.author: Ken Hanke

reviews.text: Nothing earth-shattering happens in A Separation, but the straightforwardness of this view of a disintegrating marriage, set in the context of complicated cultural and religious mors, is dramatic by itself.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: An outsider could see these characters as misguided. That's not the reality however. Farhadi slips us into their shoes and we appreciate each of their perspectives.
reviews.author: Matthew Toomey

reviews.text: The complex realities of human emotions and experience are more than sufficient to carry a film, and Farhadi doesn't let fussy direction or attempts to be overly clever get in the way of letting this brilliant, quietly insightful story unfold.
reviews.author: Ian Buckwalter

reviews.text: A clarion cry that cuts through the xenophobic clutter and the dense fog of war to show that not everyone "over there" is a boogeyman waiting to jump out of the closet. If that sounds terribly simplistic, just consider where we live.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: A Separation is more than a character study; it's a deftly plotted drama that unfolds layer after layer and will leave you asking all kinds of questions about your beliefs and moral judgments. Fascinating stuff.
reviews.author: Eric Melin

reviews.text: The story has no winners, and the daringly ambiguous ending defies simple conclusions. Even the title can be taken multiple ways.
reviews.author: Lawrence Toppman

reviews.text: The movie opens the door on a foreign culture, yet the people do not seem that dissimilar. .... They deal with some of the same struggles ... -- generational and class conflicts, ideological differences, and connecting and communicating emotionally.
reviews.author: Bob Bloom

reviews.text: A devastating portrait of two families in crisis, with their class differences representing the title's true 'separation.'
reviews.author: John Beifuss

reviews.text: "A Separation" deals with some very murky issues, but it does so with astonishing clarity.
reviews.author: Loey Lockerby

reviews.text: The movie is a singular mix of the foreign and the familiar, but is it the best 2011 film in the whole wide world? A 99? I can't say that I concur with my colleagues on that score.
reviews.author: Rick Kisonak

reviews.text: A Separation explores how presumed social norms are extremely tenuous and how threats to these almost illusory ideas can threaten our sense of personal security.
reviews.author: Thomas Caldwell

reviews.text: Farhadi does not talk down to his viewer, and he trusts his audience to make their own decisions.
reviews.author: Mark R. Leeper

reviews.text: The performances and direction match the sharply observed screenplay, which is layered and nuanced, never settling for the pat answer. Indeed, it avoids answers as much as it can, giving audiences a far more interactive experience than most films
reviews.author: Andrew L. Urban

reviews.text: Thought provoking and powerful drama. One action becomes the trigger for the unravelling that filmmaker Asghar Farhadi explores: secrets, lies and truths are exposed
reviews.author: Louise Keller

reviews.text: a brilliant, mesmerizing drama, incredibly well-acted by its ensemble cast
reviews.author: James Kendrick

reviews.text: One of A Separation's many virtues is the way it gradually reveals, Rashomon-like, the complicated facts, half-truths, and lies that each character tells for perfectly legitimate reasons.
reviews.author: Jeff Meyers

reviews.text: Finely crafted drama teems with conflicts involving class, generations, mental health and good old fashioned lying.
reviews.author: Clint O'Connor

reviews.text: These people seem so real they might live next door. And they probably do.
reviews.author: Tom Long

reviews.text: What is a sin? What is right? When is it okay to lie? All these questions swirl in a movie that might possibly be the best foreign language film at this year's Academy Awards.
reviews.author: Jonathan W. Hickman

reviews.text: "A Separation" is a plaintive fable of the human condition that unites us.
reviews.author: Joe Williams

reviews.text: One of the year's best reveals life in Iran
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: A tragically familiar family drama whose heartbreaking "for want of a nail" sequence of events spirals out of control at an intimate and individual level.
reviews.author: Duane Dudek

reviews.text: Very few movies capture as convincingly as A Separation does the ways in which seemingly honorable decisions can lead to interpersonal conflict -- even disaster.
reviews.author: Lisa Kennedy

reviews.text: Smart, provocative, and brimming with ungovernable human emotions.
reviews.author: Marjorie Baumgarten

reviews.text: To say the piercing Iranian film A Separation is about divorce is a bit like saying The Wizard of Oz is about a pair of slippers.
reviews.author: Chris Vognar

reviews.text: A meandering, nerve-wracking, ultimately worthwhile tour of contemporary Iranian urban life.
reviews.author: Kelly Vance

reviews.text: Above all, Farhadi’s parable teaches that a rush to judgment inevitably turns back on the judge.
reviews.author: Peter Canavese

reviews.text: It's a portrait of an essential and sympathetic human dilemma, and in that it's both real and timeless in ways that transcend borders, cultures and languages.
reviews.author: Shawn Levy

reviews.text: Is it possible, the movie asks, that children, with their belief in absolutes, have purer moral compasses than their forced-to-compromise parents?
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: Partly a courtroom drama, partly a political satire and partly a twisty thriller that gradually draws you in and becomes more engrossing with each new revelation.
reviews.author: John Hartl

reviews.text: Expectedly, the volatility is penetrating, but the feature is methodical, stewing in every last moment of unease and contemplation, stretching to a point where Farhadi is practically lapping himself.
reviews.author: Brian Orndorf

reviews.text: A quietly lacerating portrait of familial discord that morphs into a wider portrait of society and law...While the setting might be foreign, its concerns are universal.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: "A Separation" is a great movie, a look inside a world so foreign that it might as well be another planet, yet so universal that its observations are painfully familiar to anyone, anywhere.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: The characters are deliberately ordinary, but their stories take on the weight of myth.
reviews.author: Sam Adams

reviews.text: A gripping family drama.
reviews.author: Scott Nash

reviews.text: Ambiguous and enigmatic, it revolves around the termination of a marriage in contemporary Tehran.
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: Farhadi's carefully wrought narrative and the ways it handles the fragile emotions of its characters truly sets it apart, not only from contemporary Iranian cinema but world cinema in general.
reviews.author: Wade Major

reviews.text: What counts is that talented writer/director Asghar Farhadi structures it in a culturally compelling and mysterious way, while balancing all the characters to avoid easily typed "good guys" and "bad guys."
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: Emotionally resonant beyond the filmmaker's own country and culture, it is a compassionate yet searingly precise film that refuses to name villains, nor to let any of its protagonists off the hook
reviews.author: Andrea Chase

reviews.text: Put simply, this picture is one of the great cinematic achievements I've ever seen, and in my opinion is the best film I saw in 2011.
reviews.author: Sara Michelle Fetters

reviews.text: Sometimes, in an attempt to do the best we can for the people we love, we end up wreaking irreparable damage.
reviews.author: Rene Rodriguez

reviews.text: I hope "A Separation" is the beginning of a new cinematic dawn for Iranian filmmakers.
reviews.author: Robin Clifford

reviews.text: Asghar Farhadi's emotionally epic movie is not just a masterpiece dramatically, it is a movie dramatically of its moment.
reviews.author: John Anderson

reviews.text: [The film] puts us in the uncomfortable role of the adjudicator.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: It's small. It's real. And it's deeply moving.
reviews.author: Steven Rea

reviews.text: This is a trenchant emotional thriller that you watch in dread, awe, and amazing aggravation.
reviews.author: Wesley Morris

reviews.text: Culturally specific but universally relatable, this slowly escalating Iranian drama boasts incredibly impressive motivational clarity.
reviews.author: Matt Pais

reviews.text: Some films wear their artistry so lightly they appear simply to be happening, the inner workings of the story guided by an unseen hand.
reviews.author: Michael Phillips

reviews.text: The film involves its audience in an unusually direct way, because although we can see the logic of everyone's position, our emotions often disagree.
reviews.author: Roger Ebert

reviews.text: This is primarily a human story about a marriage unraveling, the husband torn between love for his daughter and devotion to his father, the daughter torn between one parent and the other.
reviews.author: J. R. Jones

reviews.text: It's an indictment of a culture in which religion and tradition poison a legal system. It is an exploration of the power of a lie. It is a mystery and a courtroom drama. Above all, however, it is a tale of love and sacrifice.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: For all the stifled truths of its characters, Farhadi's film feels like a gust of brisk air.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: ...like being caught in a barbed-wire fence of ethical dilemmas.
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: Feels like a peek through a neighbor's window.
reviews.author: Tricia Olszewski

reviews.text: The progressively tedious atmosphere ultimately prevents the film's final scenes from making any real emotional impact...
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: Farhadi is less concerned with the bugs and variations in human perception than cracks in the average moral compass, little fault lines that prompt good people to make bad decisions.
reviews.author: Amy Biancolli

reviews.text: In the guise of a whodunit, Farhadi paints a nuanced portrait of Iranian society that, seen through our Western eyes, looks at once utterly alien and strikingly familiar.
reviews.author: Rick Groen

reviews.text: Rashomon-like in its perceptual complexities, truth vs. belief, Asghar Farhadi's drama forces us to constantly shift our assessments and allegiances.
reviews.author: Peter Howell

reviews.text: Estabelece definitivamente Asghar Farhadi como um dos diretores mais consistentes e fascinantes do Cinema contemporneo.
reviews.author: Pablo Villaça

reviews.text: This is not the Iran that the nightly news has turned into a land of evil and inhumanity. These characters are people who love and feel anger and regret. They're simultaneously familiar and new.
reviews.author: Rob Hunter

reviews.text: Crafts a minefield out of the mundane and may very well be a masterpiece for it.
reviews.author: William Goss

reviews.text: Offers a fascinating, impartial view of modern Iran.
reviews.author: Mark Sells

reviews.text: The emotional oscillations that pulsate through A Separation -- with its tangle of unfulfilled needs, sliding values, unspoken desires, male posturing, and feminist dilemmas -- are as thrilling as the antics in any Hitchcockian thriller.
reviews.author: Brandon Judell

reviews.text: What makes it so good is that no one is bad. These humans, desperate to do right, are caught up in a perfect storm of inhumanity. The evil is in the ecosystem.
reviews.author: David Edelstein

reviews.text: An incisive look at entangled family ties in modern Iran ... where self-deceit is as pervasive in this society as anywhere else.
reviews.author: Kimberly Gadette

reviews.text: The audience is rocked back and forth in sympathy. . . in a tangled predicament. [N]one is one-dimensional in the superb ensemble [as] the point of view changes by minutes.
reviews.author: Nora Lee Mandel

reviews.text: The film wraps us, with stunning directness, in the complex folds of its characters' passions.
reviews.author: Owen Gleiberman

reviews.text: A Separation is not the work of a constrained artist. It's a great movie in which the full range of human interaction seems to play itself out before our eyes.
reviews.author: Peter Rainer

reviews.text: Farhadi's true focus is the flawed capacity for any law -- any form of cold rationality, period -- to address the slippery nature of human affairs. It's a frantic microcosm of life itself.
reviews.author: Eric Kohn

reviews.text: The miracle of A Separation is that it doesn't spare any of its characters, nor does it seek to indict them. It is a democratic portrait of a theocratic world.
reviews.author: Anthony Lane

reviews.text: Tensely involving Iranian drama with niche potential.
reviews.author: Deborah Young

reviews.text: Tense and narratively complex, formally dense and morally challenging.
reviews.author: Alissa Simon

reviews.text: A constant surprise, a film that captures the drama and suspense of real life as urgently as any picture released this year.
reviews.author: Bob Mondello

reviews.text: Simin's and Nader's divorce debate is the first of many complex issues raised and passionately argued in A Separation.
reviews.author: Richard Corliss

reviews.text: Movies with this kind of moral complexity are rare, so not only is it worth seeking out, it's one you need to see with friends because it invites -- or rather demands -- debate afterward.
reviews.author: Christy Lemire

reviews.text: Asghar Farhadi's A Separation serves as a quiet reminder of how good it's possible for movies to be.

reviews.text: So much fun to watch that you could very nearly miss the important fact that it is also as piercing a critique of Iranian society as that country has produced in some time.
reviews.author: Tim Brayton

reviews.text: There are no heroes or villains in this story: there are only everyday figures who try their best and struggle to survive.
reviews.author: Leonard Maltin

reviews.text: One of the year's most engrossing films, directed by Asghar Farhadi from his richly layered screenplay (some advice: pay particular attention to what occurs in the sequence following the opening credits)

reviews.text: A downbeat family drama of no particular distinction gradually turns into a mystery that raises painful moral questions.
reviews.author: Kyle Smith

reviews.text: It's a deceptive, Hitchcockian mystery whose clues are laid out so carefully you'll probably miss them, and a complex philosophical fable in which every character is morally compromised.
reviews.author: Andrew O'Hehir

reviews.text: It's a thrilling domestic drama that offers acute insights into human motivations and behavior as well as a compelling look at what goes on behind a particular curtain that almost never gets raised.
reviews.author: Kenneth Turan

reviews.text: Sophisticated and universal yet deeply intimate, A Separation is an exquisitely conceived family drama that has the coiled power of a top-notch thriller.
reviews.author: Claudia Puig

reviews.text: I know I wasn't expecting one of the year's best movies to come from Iran, but here it is.
reviews.author: Kurt Loder

reviews.text: It is a rigorously honest movie about the difficulties of being honest, a film that tries to be truthful about the slipperiness of truth.
reviews.author: A.O. Scott

reviews.text: While the specifics are rooted in Iranian culture, the broad strokes are entirely universal -- it's an intelligent, intriguing and inviting film.
reviews.author: Geoff Berkshire

reviews.text: grand metaphorical fiction that unpacks a weighty and involving story
reviews.author: Chris Barsanti

reviews.text: The Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film belongs right here... 'A Separation' is a landmark film. No way will you be able to get it out of your head.

reviews.text: Beyond the impeccable performances and direction, it's foremost an exceptional piece of screenwriting, so finely wrought that the drama seems guided by an invisible hand.
reviews.author: Scott Tobias

reviews.text: A richly written and performed legal procedural from Iran that enlightens as well as entertains.
reviews.author: Ethan Alter

reviews.text: Together and apart, Hatami and Maadi are magnetic.
reviews.author: Joe Neumaier

reviews.text: A movie that continually surprises you, reminding you that the best films are the ones that deal with complex emotional truth, rather than a clichd cinematic version of it.
reviews.author: Marshall Fine

reviews.text: What's fascinating is how the various issues -- religious or practical -- are played out in these two quite different families, yet always come down to irreconcilable differences between rebellious women and their stiff-necked, controlling men.

reviews.text: Far more than just the simple domestic drama it pretends to be, filled with subliminally veiled statements that add up to something with far more layers and levels.

reviews.text: ...interesting, and engaging, in both a storytelling and sociological/cultural study fashion.
reviews.author: Glenn Kenny

reviews.text: A searing Iranian film about divisiveness as a toxin in relationships.
reviews.author: Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat

reviews.text: One of the best foreign films of the year, at once particular and universal in its concerns.
reviews.author: Emanuel Levy

reviews.text: Farhadi brings us as close as can be to these characters, but he also refuses to editorialize or nudge us too far in any one direction.

reviews.text: Farhadi demonstrates a Hitchcockian flair for suspense, while his cast deliver faultless performances.
reviews.author: Lewis Porteous

reviews.text: A staggeringly sharp drama that charts the collective downfall of many different couplings after a seemingly small disagreement is made exponentially worse by denial, judgment, and guilt.
reviews.author: Glenn Heath Jr.

reviews.text: A light yet powerful Islamic family drama that refuses to cave in to stereotypes.
reviews.author: Ron Wilkinson

reviews.text: If it feels familiar, it's because it's as poignant, precarious, and endlessly complicated as life itself.
reviews.author: Elise Nakhnikian

reviews.text: A solid Iranian Oscar-entry that puts women in the forefront in a battle of wills that happily posits more questions than answers.

reviews.text: "A Separation" could hardly be more concrete, or contemporary, or dramatic.
reviews.author: Joe Morgenstern

reviews.text: It resonates deeply thanks to its universality, which it miraculously achieves without ever once selling out the social mores of its location. Profoundly affecting, wonderfully performed and endlessly surprising.

reviews.text: A masterpiece of intimate, dramatic filmmaking.

reviews.text: A remarkably poised marital thriller from Iran, full of surprise developments and suppressed volatility.

reviews.text: A stunning piece of work, beautifully telling a raw human story with expert writing, direction, photography, editing and acting

reviews.text: This is a movie that makes you pay attention to action and consequences in a way that has more or less completely disappeared from mainstream cinema.

reviews.text: It's well acted, thoughtful, using a realistically messy scenario to draw together strong central themes. Unusual and well worth a look.

reviews.text: A bit of a slog, although fresh and even lyric in moments.

reviews.text: Cleverly, as new details emerge about what REALLY happened, your sympathy lurches from side to side like Amy Winehouse doing Back To Black at the Belgrade Alhambra.

synopsis: When Nader (Payman Maadi), a bank employee, refuses to leave Tehran, his wife, Simin (Leila Hatami) sues for divorce in the hope that she can make a better life for their young daughter abroad. Needing someone to care for his senile father while he's at work, Nader hires Razieh (Sareh Bayat), a married woman whose chador hides her pregnancy. One day, after becoming angry with Razieh, Nader shoves her, and she has a miscarriage, leading Razieh's husband to take Nader to court.
